Concrete Driveways · Oviedo, FL

Pouring or Replacing a Concrete Driveway in Oviedo

A new or replacement concrete driveway in Oviedo runs $6–$15 per sq ft installed as of October 2026. Inside the city, the private portion is reviewed separately from the apron crossing into the right-of-way, which carries its own $104 application fee; in unincorporated Seminole County, the whole driveway instead goes through a single county application capped at 18 feet wide.

By the Opera Concrete & Pavers estimating team · Updated October 1, 2026

Inside Oviedo, the apron gets its own $104 right-of-way review

Where a driveway meets the street, that section falls under the city's Right-of-Way Type I application, filed with the Development Review Division at 400 Alexandria Blvd., 407-971-5796. The current form, revised October 2023, totals $104.00, a $79.00 application fee plus a $25.00 technology fee, and the city also wants a sealed boundary survey, a maintenance-of-traffic plan and proof of insurance before it signs off (City of Oviedo, Right-of-Way Type I Application). The rest of the slab on private ground is a separate planning and zoning permit, since Oviedo's own 2026 exemption list keeps driveways on private property out of the building-permit exemption HB 803 otherwise created (City of Oviedo, Building Services).

Timing the Saw Cut Changes What the Joint Looks Like

A control joint cut too late can miss the crack it was meant to control, and one cut too early can tear the surface instead of slicing it cleanly. Early-entry saws go in about 1 to 4 hours after finishing, while a conventional wet saw waits 4 to 12 hours until the concrete has firmed up enough to cut without ravelling the edge. The right window shifts with temperature and humidity on a given Oviedo pour day, which is why we watch the slab rather than work off a fixed clock. Getting this step wrong shows up later as a ragged joint edge or a crack that wandered off the cut line.

A two-car driveway crossing the right-of-way, worked out in square feet

Picture a 24 by 22 ft two-car driveway, 528 sq ft, replacing an original slab on a lot inside the Oviedo city limits. At $6–$15 per sq ft installed, the private portion lands between roughly $3,168 and $7,920 before demolition is added. A 9 by 5 ft section of that same driveway, 45 sq ft, sits in the right-of-way where it meets the street, and that piece adds the separate $104 Right-of-Way Type I fee on top of the per-square-foot driveway cost, along with the survey and traffic-control plan the city asks for before approving it. On an otherwise identical lot in unincorporated Seminole County, that same width clears the county's 18-foot cap without a conditional review.

Outside the city, one county application sets the width at 18 feet

A lot carrying an Oviedo address can still sit in unincorporated Seminole County, where the Residential Driveway Construction Application caps a driveway at 18 feet wide, 24 feet counting the 3-foot flares on each side, and requires 6 inches of non-steel or fiber-reinforced concrete at 3,000 psi inside the right-of-way (Seminole County, Residential Driveway Construction Application). That review runs through the county's Development Review Division (Plandesk@seminolecountyfl.gov, 407-665-7371) rather than the city desk, and a driveway planned wider than 18 feet on an unincorporated lot is worth confirming against that cap before a paver driveway or a wide concrete apron gets designed.

Irrigation Heads Aimed at the Driveway Cause Slow Damage

A sprinkler head that has drifted even slightly over the years can end up soaking the edge of a driveway every time the zone runs, and that repeated wetting works against a compacted base the same way standing rainwater would, just more predictably. It also leaves mineral staining on the concrete surface that gets worse with every cycle. On a Oviedo lot, it is worth checking irrigation head aim against the new driveway's footprint before the first watering cycle after the pour, since a head that was fine aimed at an old garden bed is not necessarily fine aimed at fresh concrete and a compacted edge that has not fully settled yet.

What a Flatwoods Lot Means for the Subgrade

Much of Greater Orlando and the Suncoast sits on flatwoods soil series like Myakka, Smyrna, Immokalee, EauGallie and Pomona, which hold a water table within 18 inches of the surface for one to four months most years. That is workable ground for a driveway, but only if we test it before pouring instead of assuming it behaves like the lot next door. Wet, weak native soil will not compact to a stable subgrade no matter how long a plate compactor runs over it. On a Oviedo property with this kind of soil, we remove the saturated layer and build up with compacted fill rather than forming directly on soggy ground, which is what keeps the slab from settling unevenly within a few years.

Why the Saw Comes Out Hours, Not Days, After the Pour

Joint cutting happens on a tight clock relative to the pour, not on a separate visit days later. Depending on the saw and the weather, cuts go in anywhere from about 1 hour to about 12 hours after finishing, timed to when the concrete has firmed up enough to cut cleanly without the edge crumbling. On a Oviedo job, we track the slab's set time rather than work from a fixed schedule, since a hot, dry afternoon firms concrete up faster than an overcast one. Missing that window in either direction is how a joint ends up ragged or badly placed relative to where the slab actually wants to crack.

A Driveway on Flatwoods Soil Needs Drainage Checked Every Wet Season

Flatwoods soils like Myakka and Smyrna hold water close to the surface for months at a stretch during the wetter part of the year, which means a driveway built on that kind of lot depends on its original grading continuing to shed water the way it was designed to. Mulch beds, new landscaping or a few years of settling can quietly change how water moves across a Oviedo yard and start directing runoff back toward the slab instead of away from it. Checking that the grading still slopes the right way each time the yard changes is cheap insurance against the kind of slow saturation that got the base into trouble in the first place.

Frequently asked questions

Does Oviedo charge a separate fee for the part of my driveway that meets the street?

Yes. The Right-of-Way Type I application covers that section, $79.00 plus a $25.00 technology fee, $104.00 total, filed with the Development Review Division along with a sealed survey, a traffic-control plan and proof of insurance.

How wide can a driveway be in unincorporated Seminole County?

The county's Residential Driveway Construction Application caps an ordinary driveway at 18 feet wide, 24 feet including the 3-foot flares on each side, reviewed by the Development Review Division rather than the city.

Does Oviedo's 2026 permit exemption cover a new driveway?

No. The city's own list of work that still needs a planning and zoning permit names “pavers/driveways/sidewalks on private property” directly, so HB 803's $7,500 building-permit exemption doesn't reach a driveway inside the city limits.
